questions.q: What is a cloud management platform / brokerage layer, as described in this lesson?
options: A replacement for Azure Resource Manager and the AWS control plane
A tool that pulls data from each provider's native APIs (billing, policy) into one aggregated interface, without replacing any provider's own control plane
A feature built directly into AWS Organizations
A new cloud provider that competes with Azure and AWS
questions.explain: Products like CloudHealth, Flexera One, and Morpheus Data consume the same billing and policy APIs an engineer could query directly, and present the aggregated result in one interface — they don't replace the underlying providers' control planes.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three things this lesson says a brokerage layer genuinely adds?
options: It makes AWS S3 and Azure Blob Storage share an identical API
It eliminates the need for any tagging taxonomy
It guarantees a lower cloud bill automatically
A single pane of glass for cost that does FOCUS-style normalization and ingestion automatically instead of by hand
questions.explain: The three real additions named in the lesson are a unified cost pane of glass, unified chargeback/showback reporting, and a consolidated governance view — automating work that would otherwise be manual.

questions.q: What is the central limitation of a cloud brokerage layer that this lesson emphasizes?
options: It only works with Azure, never AWS
It cannot be used for governance reporting, only cost
It cannot make the underlying cloud services (e.g., Blob Storage vs. S3) operationally or technically equivalent — differing APIs, consistency models, and IAM still remain
It requires every resource to be moved into the brokerage vendor's own cloud
questions.explain: No dashboard changes the fact that Azure Blob Storage, AWS S3, and on-prem storage have genuinely different APIs, consistency guarantees, and IAM models; a brokerage layer displays data about the difference but doesn't erase it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe adopting a brokerage platform as 'a cost decision too'?
options: Because brokerage platforms are always free for enterprises
Because it carries its own license cost, integration-maintenance burden, and staffing need, which can exceed the cost of a lighter in-house normalization pipeline for a smaller footprint
Because only on-prem infrastructure has any real cost
Because brokerage platforms replace the need for any cloud spend at all
questions.explain: A brokerage platform is a build-vs-buy decision: its license and upkeep cost can outweigh the benefit for a smaller multi-cloud estate, so it should be chosen deliberately rather than assumed to be an automatic win.

questions.q: In the governance use of a brokerage layer, what does it actually surface?
options: A brand-new, independent policy engine that overrides Azure Policy and AWS Config
Only on-prem compliance data, since cloud governance is out of scope
Violations from Azure Policy and AWS Config/SCPs side by side, mapped back to one shared control catalog, rather than checking two separate consoles
Nothing related to governance — brokerage tools are cost-only
questions.explain: The consolidated governance view pulls existing violations from each provider's native policy engine into one place, mapped to the same control catalog, rather than replacing those native engines.
